passport_validity_required.value: Valid at least 3 months beyond your intended departure from the Schengen area, and issued within the last 10 years
passport_validity_required.notes: 3-month rule confirmed on the official State Dept Spain page 2026-06-12; the 10-year-issuance rule is the standard Schengen condition

onward_ticket_required.value: Border officers MAY ask for proof of onward/return travel and sufficient funds — formally part of entry conditions, rarely demanded of American tourists in practice. Have your return booking accessible
onward_ticket_required.notes: Sources split (deepseek: no, gemini: yes); resolved as the nuanced truth — both oversimplified

notes.value: Spanish law requires carrying ID — passport or at minimum a copy/photo; hotels must register your passport at check-in (normal, not a scam). EES biometrics on first entry since Oct 2025. Bring physical insurance documents

approx_rate_note.notes: VOLATILE — never freeze USD↔EUR; pull live at write time

cash_vs_card.value: Card-dominant: Visa/Mastercard with contactless and Apple/Google Pay work nearly everywhere, including the metro and tapas bars; Amex is hit-or-miss. Carry €20-40 cash for tiny bars, market stalls, small tips. ALWAYS choose to pay in EUR — decline DCC ('pay in dollars') on every terminal and ATM

atm_availability.value: Everywhere. Use bank-branded ATMs (CaixaBank, Santander, BBVA, Sabadell) and decline conversion; avoid Euronet and other standalone tourist ATMs — predatory rates and fees

currency_import_export_limit.value: €10,000 or equivalent in cash entering/leaving the EU must be declared
currency_import_export_limit.notes: Threshold confirmed on the official State Dept Spain page 2026-06-12

tipping_norm.value: Not expected — servers earn standard wages. Round up or leave a few coins casually; 5-10% at a nice dinner is generous; nothing at the bar; round up taxis. Card terminals don't prompt for tips, and that's normal. Never tip US-style 15-20%

Girona (GRO) and Reus (REU) — distant budget-carrier airports ~1-1.5h away, almost exclusively intra-Europe; never book these thinking they're 'Barcelona'

United seasonal; otherwise one-stop via East Coast or EU hubs
LEVEL has operated the route; often cheaper one-stop

flight_from_audience_origins.notes: Durations stable-ish; PRICES + the exact seasonal route map are serve_live — verify current schedules before the flights article

intercity_rail.value: Excellent high-speed network from Barcelona Sants: Renfe AVE plus low-cost competitors Ouigo, iryo and Avlo. Madrid ~2h30-3h; Girona ~38min; Camp de Tarragona ~35min; Figueres-Vilafant ~55min. Book high-speed ahead for the best fares; Rodalies commuter lines cover Sitges and the coast

buses.value: ALSA for long-distance intercity; regional Catalonia operators (Moventis/Sarfa, Sagalés, Monbus) from Estació del Nord cover Costa Brava coves the trains don't reach

domestic_flights.value: Skip them to Madrid — high-speed rail wins door-to-door on that route. Flying genuinely beats the train for destinations rail can't reach quickly: Seville (~1h20 flight on Iberia/Vueling vs ~5h30+ train, no direct high-speed line), the Canary Islands (rail doesn't reach them at all), and to a lesser extent Bilbao (~1h25 flight vs ~6h train) when a trip extends beyond this site's Catalonia/Madrid scope. Within Catalonia and to Madrid, AVE wins on total door-to-door time once airport transfer and security are factored in; the calculus flips only once a destination is far enough that rail has no fast direct option.
domestic_flights.notes: Route/duration comparisons are Claude general-knowledge synthesis, not independently source-verified this round — flag as verify_recommended; exact flight schedules and fares are serve_live regardless.

ticketing_across_operators.value: VERIFIED 2026-09-07 (fetched seat61.com + corroborated via Trainline) — there is NO unified through-ticket across competing operators: Renfe AVE, Ouigo, iryo and Avlo each require a SEPARATE ticket, even when transferring between them on the same trip. The one exception is 'Combinado Cercanías': buying a Renfe long-distance ticket OR an iryo ticket includes a FREE connecting Cercanías (suburban) ride at both ends of the journey, valid roughly 3-4 hours before departure and after arrival, within designated urban zones (Barcelona, Madrid, Valencia, etc.) — scan the long-distance ticket's QR at the Cercanías gate, or collect a paper Cercanías ticket. This free-connection perk does NOT extend to Ouigo or Avlo tickets.
ticketing_across_operators.notes: Two independent sources agree (seat61.com, a well-regarded independent rail-travel authority, and Trainline's own operator page).

ride_sharing.value: Uber, Cabify and Bolt all work in Barcelona — largely dispatching licensed taxis and VTC at regulated rates, so don't expect US-style discounts. Official black-and-yellow taxis are plentiful, metered, reliable; FreeNow hails them by app

transport_strikes.value: VERIFIED 2026-09-07 (fetched timeout.com + euroweeklynews.com/democrata.es coverage of actual 2026 Renfe strikes) — Spanish law (under the strike-rights framework of Royal Decree-Law 17/1977) requires transport operators to run MINIMUM SERVICES even during a strike, typically 50-75% of normal capacity depending on route/time (e.g. a recent AVE/long-distance strike ran at 73% capacity; Cercanías commuter trains are protected at 75% in peak hours, dropping to 50% off-peak) — so a strike thins service, it essentially never stops it entirely. Under EU passenger-rights law, a traveler whose train is cancelled due to strike action is entitled to a full refund within 30 days, or can rebook at no extra cost, regardless of how the ticket was purchased. Check for planned strikes via the specific operator's own site/app (Renfe, Ouigo, iryo each post their own cancelled-service lists) rather than a generic news search, since minimum-service schedules are set per strike.
transport_strikes.notes: Legal framework + passenger rights corroborated across timeout.com and multiple 2026 strike-specific news reports (euroweeklynews, democrata.es). Whether/when a strike is happening on the traveler's specific dates is inherently serve_live — never claim to know current strike status from this fact.

car_rental_and_driving.value: Drive on the right. US license + International Driving Permit (IDP) legally REQUIRED for US drivers in Spain (get it from AAA before flying — ~$20). BAC limit 0.05% (0.03% novice) — stricter than US norms. Do NOT rent a car for Barcelona itself: low-emission zone (ZBE), scarce $35+/night parking, break-in risk; rent only for a Costa Brava day, picking up on departure day
car_rental_and_driving.notes: driving side, license/IDP, BAC limit. deepseek dissented ('IDP recommended'); kept REQUIRED per Spanish DGT rule + claude/gemini agreement

car_rental_desk_practices.value: ADDED 2026-09-07 — general car-rental-industry knowledge, not Spain-specific verification. Beyond the legal requirements above, expect standard rental-desk practices: a hold (not charge) on a credit card for the deposit/excess, sized to the vehicle's damage excess — a DEBIT card is often refused outright for this hold. Desk staff routinely upsell their own collision-damage-waiver insurance at a markup over what a third-party excess-insurance policy (bought before the trip) costs for the same coverage — buying third-party cover in advance is usually the better value if you're comfortable with the paperwork of a post-trip reimbursement claim. Fuel policy is typically 'full-to-full' (return with a full tank or pay a penalty rate) — the fairest option when offered a choice. Cross-border restrictions are common and easy to miss: confirm explicitly if you plan to cross into France or Andorra, since some Spain-based rentals restrict or surcharge this.

accident_procedure.value: ADDED 2026-09-07 — standard EU/Spain procedure, general knowledge. After any accident: ensure safety first (hazard lights, safety vests — legally required in the car, warning triangle), then exchange information using the European Accident Statement form ('parte amistoso de accidente' / constat amiable) that most rental cars carry in the glovebox — both drivers fill and sign it, and it's the standard document insurers on both sides expect. Call 112 for any injury, significant damage, or dispute about fault; for a minor no-injury fender-bender with agreement on fault, many rentals don't require police attendance at all, but call your rental company's emergency assistance line either way — it's usually printed on the rental agreement — before doing anything else with the vehicle. Take photos of both vehicles, all visible damage, the other party's license/insurance/rental agreement, and the surrounding scene before moving anything. Never sign anything you don't understand — ask for an English copy or photograph the document to have translated later.

e_scooters_barcelona.value: VERIFIED 2026-09-07 (fetched barcelona.cat official mobility page + corroborated by catalannews.com and a specialized EU e-scooter law site) — Barcelona's municipal ordinance on personal mobility vehicles (VMP) requires: a HELMET for every rider, mandatory since February 1, 2025 (a real, enforced, current rule, not a recommendation); NO riding on sidewalks/pedestrian areas under any circumstance — a €500 fine; riding is confined to bike lanes (25 km/h max on road-level lanes), pavement-level cycle paths (10 km/h max), zona-30 streets, and designated park routes (10 km/h max); one rider per scooter only; front/rear lights, a working brake light, and a horn/bell are required equipment; insurance is mandatory for e-scooter riders under Spain's Automobile Insurance Act, in force since July 25, 2025; parking is restricted to designated scooter parking spaces only (not locked to random street furniture). This applies to both privately-owned and shared/rental scooters.
e_scooters_barcelona.notes: Corroborated across the official city page, catalannews.com's coverage of the Feb 2025 regulation change, and a specialized e-scooter law reference site. Fines/exact enforcement intensity can shift; re-verify the €500 figure at write time.

travel_insurance_activity_exclusions.value: ADDED 2026-09-07 — general travel/rental insurance-policy pattern, not a Spain-specific legal rule; verify against the SPECIFIC policy in question before publishing a firm claim. Common activities that void or complicate a standard travel/rental-car insurance claim: driving a rental car WITHOUT the legally required IDP (ties directly to car_rental_and_driving above — a claim can be denied on this technicality even if the accident itself wasn't your fault); riding a moped, motorcycle, or e-scooter without the license class that vehicle actually requires under Spanish law; certain 'extreme' or high-risk activities (cliff-diving, some watersports, off-piste equivalents) that a standard policy excludes by name — always the specific policy's exclusions list, not a generic assumption; and, for e-scooters specifically, riding without the insurance now mandated under Spain's Automobile Insurance Act (see e_scooters_barcelona) can itself be a policy violation on top of being illegal.

climate_by_season.value: Mediterranean. Spring (Mar-May) 55-72°F, ideal; Summer (Jun-Aug) 75-90°F and humid — feels stickier than the number, busiest, sea warm; Fall (Sep-Oct) 65-80°F, ideal, sea still swimmable; Winter (Nov-Feb) 45-60°F, mild and mostly sunny, quietest. Rain comes in short bursts, mostly spring/fall

shoulder_season_tradeoffs.value: May, June, September, October are the shoulder months (also the unanimous best_months pick). What you trade for the lower crowds/prices vs peak summer: hotel rates typically run noticeably below July-August peak (exact % is serve_live, varies by property and year — never freeze a number); sights are meaningfully less crowded, especially before 10am; sea is swimmable May-Oct (warmest Jul-Sep, genuinely pleasant by June and still swimmable into October per climate_by_season); a few outdoor/seasonal offerings (some beach-club style venues, certain extended summer hours at attractions) scale back outside Jun-Aug; rain risk is somewhat higher in spring/fall than in the dry summer stretch, in short bursts rather than all-day. May/June trades slightly cooler sea + a small rain-risk bump for the lowest crowds of the four; September/October trades slightly shorter daylight for the warmest sea of the shoulder window and the tail of summer energy.
shoulder_season_tradeoffs.notes: RECOMMENDATION, Claude-authored synthesis of existing when_to_go data — not a checkable legal/procedural fact, so not run through the external panel. No source needed for a judgment call; specific numeric price deltas deliberately omitted as serve_live.

main_risk.value: Pickpocketing and bag-snatching — Barcelona's one genuine, daily, NON-violent risk; thieves are skilled professionals, not muggers. Hotspots: Las Ramblas, the metro (esp. L3 and airport runs), Sagrada Família crowds, the beach (never leave anything unattended), terrace chair-backs. Violent crime against tourists is rare. Tone for articles: honest, not alarmist — preventable with habits

shopping_crafts._note: ADDED 2026-09-07 for buying-ceramics-in-spain-getting-it-home. General/cultural knowledge, low YMYL stakes — Claude-authored, no external panel run.

ceramics_overview.value: Spain has several distinct ceramics traditions, not one 'Spanish ceramic' style — the honest framing for an article is regional, not national. Catalonia's own tradition centers on La Bisbal d'Empordà (near Girona, roughly 1.5-2h from Barcelona), a town whose main street is lined with ceramics workshops and showrooms; further afield, Talavera de la Puebla (near Toledo) and Manises (near Valencia) are Spain's other major ceramics centers, both well outside this site's Catalonia/Barcelona scope. Within Barcelona itself, ceramics are sold at craft markets (Fira de Santa Llúcia at Christmas, occasional artisan markets), some El Born and Gràcia boutiques carrying Catalan and imported Spanish pieces, and gift shops attached to major sights.

us_customs_on_spanish_purchases.value: VERIFY_RECOMMENDED 2026-09-07 (corroborated across multiple sources — a USDA/APHIS approved-establishments document, a first-hand enforcement account, and independent travel-forum discussion — but the primary APHIS regulation text itself could not be directly opened this round, PDF parsing failed) — under 9 CFR 94.31, cured hams (jamón ibérico, jamón serrano, similar products) from Spain, France, Germany and Italy may NOT be brought into the US by travelers in personal luggage; they can only enter as commercial shipments from USDA/FDA-approved Spanish processing establishments, which is not the path an individual tourist buying from a shop or market uses. This catches Americans off guard constantly since jamón is one of Spain's most iconic purchases. Beyond meat products, ordinary US personal customs exemptions apply to typical souvenir purchases (the standard personal exemption threshold, duty on anything above it) — nothing else Spain-specific beyond the meat-product restriction.
us_customs_on_spanish_purchases.notes: Re-verify the exact regulation citation and current exemption dollar threshold directly on aphis.gov/cbp.gov before publishing as a hard rule — the meat-product restriction itself is well-corroborated, but the primary source document didn't parse cleanly this round.

buying_and_shipping.value: For a small piece (a bowl, tiles, a small vase), wrap it in clothing inside a carry-on rather than checking it — airline baggage handling is the single biggest breakage risk. For larger or more valuable pieces, ask the shop about shipping directly (many workshops in ceramics towns like La Bisbal ship internationally routinely) rather than trying to hand-carry something fragile and awkward through several more flight legs. There's no special Spanish export restriction on contemporary ceramics for personal purchase — the ordinary US customs personal-exemption and duty rules for goods apply, same as any souvenir.
buying_and_shipping.notes: Shipping/customs framing is general-knowledge synthesis; if a specific reader question about duty thresholds comes up, that's a US customs fact (already covered generally elsewhere in the site's practical-info coverage), not a Spain-side export rule.

how_to_get_there.value: From BCN airport: Aerobús A1/A2 every ~5-10min to Pl. Catalunya, ~35min — €7.45 single / €12.85 round-trip per the OFFICIAL operator fare (Mar 2026; resellers quote more with extras; link aerobusbarcelona.es). Metro L9 Sud needs a special ~€5.15 airport ticket (T-casual not valid) and no direct center run — transfer, ~1h total. Rodalies R2 Nord from T2 (~25min to Sants/Passeig de Gràcia, ~€4-5; free T1↔T2 shuttle). Taxi ~€35-45 to center, 25-35min. ALL FARES serve_live — refresh before the airport article
how_to_get_there.notes: Aerobús fare verified against the operator 2026-06-12 after a 3-way source conflict; treat every number as serve_live

local_transport.value: TMB metro + buses + FGC, fully integrated. T-casual (10 rides, zone 1, ~€12-12.15) is the first-timer workhorse — personal, not shareable; Hola Barcelona unlimited passes (48-120h, INCLUDES airport metro); T-mobilitat contactless rollout ongoing. Single rides are poor value. Metro ~5:00-midnight, later Fri, all night Sat. Walking covers Gòtic/Born/Raval; the Eixample grid is bigger than it looks
local_transport.notes: T-casual price change-prone — verify before the metro article

airport.value: Josep Tarradellas Barcelona–El Prat (BCN), ~8 miles SW. T1 = legacy carriers incl. US nonstops; T2 = mostly budget. Free green shuttle between terminals

sagrada_familia_visit_logistics.value: RESOLVED 2026-09-06 (was an open question) — fetched sagradafamilia.org directly. Only the Nativity facade tower and the Passion facade tower are offered to visitors (elevator up, stairs down, not accessible for reduced mobility); the central Jesus Christ tower is NOT among the visitor tower options on the official site — no evidence it is climbable. Tickets currently open roughly 2 months ahead of the visit date. Entry involves a security screening (metal detectors, bag checks); lockers are available only for small bags/rucksacks needed to free your hands for the tower visit, NOT for suitcases. Tickets are valid only for their exact time slot — arriving late means no entry, no exceptions, no official guidance on how many minutes early to arrive. A quiet hour runs 9:00-10:00am (headphones required for audio, guests asked to stay quiet). Dress code: no see-through clothing or swimwear; shoulders must be covered in some chapel areas (consistent with the site's existing dress_norms).
sagrada_familia_visit_logistics.notes: Also checked https://sagradafamilia.org/en/faqs and https://sagradafamilia.org/en/tickets for corroboration. Booking-window and tower-access figures should still be re-checked at write time per the site's own serve_live discipline (official pages can change), but this is a real, current, directly-fetched source, not panel consensus.

Practical, not pretty: built around Barcelona Sants station — the pick for an early train/AVE departure or a late arrival, direct airport train (R2 Nord) access, and reliably cheaper rates than the old-town areas. Residential and a bit characterless compared to Gràcia or El Born; you're trading atmosphere for logistics. Right choice for a one-night pre-departure stay or a budget-first trip; wrong choice if soaking up neighborhood atmosphere matters to you.
